lessons.title: Lesson 1: Choosing the safest water source
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Rank the water sources near your home from safest to riskiest.
This lesson builds toward: Given the water sources near your home, you will rank the water sources from safest to riskiest and choose one for drinking, giving a reason for each one and naming a back-up source.
Water can look clear and still carry germs. The biggest danger is faeces (human or animal waste) getting into the water. WHO says unsafe water can spread diarrhoea, cholera, dysentery, typhoid, hepatitis A and polio. Water from rivers and lakes can also carry worms that cause bilharzia (schistosomiasis).
Safer sources are usually piped water, a protected borehole or well with a cover and a pump, protected springs and rainwater collected in a clean, covered tank. Riskier sources are open wells, unprotected springs, rivers, ponds, lakes and dams, where people and animals wash, swim and drink. Water from a kiosk, tanker or sachet is only as safe as where it came from and how it was handled.
Look at each source near you. Is it covered? Is there a toilet, latrine or animal pen close to it, or uphill of it? Do people wash clothes or let animals drink there? Choose the safest one for drinking and cooking, and a back-up for when it is dry or broken. Even good water can get dirty on the way home, so you will still treat and store it well (next lessons).
Step by step:
- List every water source your family uses.
- For each one ask: is it covered, protected and away from toilets and animals?
- Rank them from safest to riskiest.
- Choose one for drinking and cooking, and a back-up.
- Use riskier water only for washing, and still treat any water you drink.
Words to know:
- Faeces: human or animal waste (poo).
- Protected source: a well, borehole or spring that is covered and sealed so dirt and runoff cannot get in.
- Bilharzia (schistosomiasis): an illness from tiny worms in some rivers and lakes.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Drinking-water fact sheet
Try it now: Write down every water source your family uses. Mark each one safer or riskier, and why. Circle the one you will use for drinking and the back-up.
You can now compare the water sources near you and choose the safest one for drinking, with a back-up.

check.q: Which source is usually safest for drinking?
options: A protected borehole with a cover and pump
A dam where people wash clothes
check.why: A protected, covered source keeps faeces and runoff out.

check.q: The river water looks clear. What is true?
options: Clear water can still carry germs, so treat it before drinking
check.why: Germs cannot be seen; clear water can still carry them.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Making drinking water safer at home
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Make drinking water safer by boiling it or with a chlorine product sold for water.
This lesson builds toward: Given water from your source and the things you have at home, you will make drinking water safer by boiling it or with a chlorine product sold for water, following every step, including settling or filtering cloudy water first and following the product label.
If your water may not be safe, treat it before drinking, before mixing baby food or formula, and before brushing teeth. Two common ways are boiling and chlorine. Both work best on clear water.
If the water is cloudy, first let it settle in a clean container so dirt sinks to the bottom, then pour the clear water off through a clean cloth folded several times. Settling and cloth filtering do not make water safe on their own; they prepare it for boiling or chlorine.
Boiling: bring the water to a rolling boil, with big bubbles, for 1 minute. High in the mountains, above about 2,000 metres, boil for 3 minutes. Let it cool, covered, in the same pot or a clean container.
Chlorine: use a chlorine product sold for drinking water (liquid, tablets or sachets) or one your health worker gives. Follow the label exactly: how much for how much water, and how long to wait before drinking (often at least 30 minutes). Cloudy water may need more; the label tells you. Keep chlorine away from children. If you have no label or are unsure, ask your community health worker or clinic. WHO tests some household water treatment products; your ministry of health can say which are approved where you live.
Step by step:
- If cloudy: let it settle, then pour it through a clean folded cloth.
- Boil: a rolling boil for 1 minute (3 minutes high in the mountains), then cool it covered.
- Or chlorine: add the product as its label says, stir, and wait the time on the label.
- Pour it into a clean, covered container.
- Keep chlorine products out of children's reach.
Words to know:
- Rolling boil: water boiling hard with big bubbles that do not stop when you stir.
- Chlorine product: a liquid, tablet or sachet sold to kill germs in drinking water.
- Settle: leave water still so dirt sinks to the bottom.
Official sources:
- US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): How to make water safe (boiling, settling and filtering, disinfecting)
- World Health Organization: Drinking-water fact sheet
Try it now: Choose one way, boiling or a chlorine product, and treat one container of drinking water today, step by step. Write down each step you did.
You can now make cloudy or doubtful water safer to drink by settling, then boiling or using a chlorine product as its label says.

check.q: Your water is cloudy. What do you do before boiling or adding chlorine?
options: Let it settle and pour it through a clean folded cloth
check.why: Settling and filtering remove dirt so boiling or chlorine work better.

check.q: How long do you keep water at a rolling boil at normal heights?
check.why: CDC advises a rolling boil for 1 minute, or 3 minutes high in the mountains.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Storing and serving water safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Store and serve drinking water so hands and dirt cannot touch it.
This lesson builds toward: Given treated water and the containers in your home, you will store and serve drinking water so hands and dirt do not touch it, using a clean covered container and pouring or using a tap, never dipping.
Safe water can get dirty again in the home. Germs get in when hands or cups are dipped into the container, when it is left open, or when the container itself is dirty.
Keep drinking water in a clean container with a lid, ideally with a narrow neck or a tap. Keep it off the floor and away from animals. Pour water out or use the tap; never dip a cup or your hand in. Wash the container and lid with soap and safe water often, and let it dry upside down.
Covering water also stops mosquitoes laying eggs in it. Keep drinking water apart from water for washing. A family in Kumasi, Lubumbashi or Kano can use the same rule: one clean, covered drinking-water container per home, and nobody dips.
Step by step:
- Use a clean container with a lid, narrow neck or tap.
- Keep it raised off the floor, away from animals.
- Pour or use the tap: no dipping cups or hands.
- Wash the container with soap and safe water often.
- Keep drinking water separate from washing water.
Words to know:
- Container: a jerrycan, bucket, pot or bottle that holds water.
- Dipping: putting a cup or hand into the water to take some out.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Drinking-water fact sheet
- US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC): How to make water safe (boiling, settling and filtering, disinfecting)
Try it now: Look at how your home stores drinking water. Is it covered? Does anyone dip? Make one change today, such as a lid, a ladle with a long handle kept on a hook, or a container with a tap.
You can now store and serve drinking water so it stays clean after you treat it.

check.q: What is the safest way to take water from the storage container?
options: Pour it out or use a tap
Leave the lid off so it is quick
check.why: Pouring or using a tap keeps hands and cups out of the clean water.

check.q: Why keep a lid on the drinking-water container?
options: It keeps out dirt, hands and mosquitoes
check.why: A lid stops dirt, germs and mosquito eggs getting in.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Clean hands, safe toilets, quick action

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Handwashing with soap at the key times
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Wash hands with soap at the key times and set up a handwashing place at home.
This lesson builds toward: Given soap or ash and water at home, you will wash hands with soap at the key times and set up a handwashing place, scrubbing every part of the hands for at least 20 seconds, with the station near the toilet and the kitchen.
Washing hands with soap is one of the cheapest ways to stop diarrhoea and chest infections. Water alone is not enough; soap lifts the germs off.
Key times: after using the toilet; after cleaning a child's bottom or changing a nappy; before, during and after preparing food; before eating and before feeding a child; after caring for someone sick with diarrhoea or vomiting; after blowing your nose, coughing or sneezing; and after touching animals or rubbish.
How: wet your hands with clean running water, add soap, rub the palms, the backs, between the fingers and under the nails for at least 20 seconds (about as long as singing a short song twice), rinse in running water and let them air-dry or use a clean cloth. Where there is no tap, a handwashing station helps: a jerrycan or bottle with a small hole and a stopper, hung or tipped with a foot stick (often called a tippy tap), with soap on a string and a little gravel underneath for the waste water. Put it near the toilet and near where you cook.
Step by step:
- Wet hands with clean running water.
- Add soap.
- Scrub palms, backs, between fingers and under nails for at least 20 seconds.
- Rinse in running water.
- Air-dry or use a clean cloth.
- Set up a station near the toilet and the kitchen.
Words to know:
- Key times: the moments when washing hands stops the most germs.
- Handwashing station: a fixed place with water and soap for washing hands.
- Tippy tap: a simple handwashing station made from a jerrycan or bottle that you tip with a foot pedal.
Official sources:
- CDC: About handwashing (key times and steps)
- World Health Organization: Drinking-water fact sheet
Try it now: Set up or improve one handwashing place at home today, with water and soap, near the toilet or the kitchen. Then show each person in your home how to wash for 20 seconds.
You can now wash hands well with soap at the key times and set up a handwashing place at home.

check.q: When must you wash your hands with soap?
options: After the toilet, after cleaning a child's bottom and before cooking or eating
check.why: These key times stop germs from faeces reaching food and mouths.

check.q: How long should you scrub with soap?
options: At least 20 seconds, all parts of the hands
check.why: Scrubbing every part for at least 20 seconds removes the germs.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Safe toilets and children's faeces
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Keep your toilet clean and dispose of children's faeces safely.
This lesson builds toward: Given your toilet or latrine and young children at home, you will keep the toilet clean and dispose of children's faeces safely, with no faeces left in the open and a lid or cover in use.
Faeces left in the open, in a bush, a field, a drain or a river, carry germs that flies, feet, rain and hands bring back to food and water. WHO and UNICEF count a toilet as safer when it separates faeces from people: a flush or pour-flush toilet, or a pit latrine with a slab. A toilet your household does not share is better still.
Keep the toilet or latrine clean: wash the slab or seat often, keep the lid or cover on the hole to keep flies off, and keep a handwashing place right next to it. Children need a toilet they can use safely too, such as a potty or a small hole cover.
Young children's faeces are as dangerous as adults'. Put them in the toilet or latrine straight away, including from nappies and potties, then wash the potty and your hands with soap. Do not leave them in the yard or throw them into the drain or rubbish.
Step by step:
- Wash the slab or seat often.
- Keep the lid or cover on the hole.
- Keep soap and water right next to the toilet.
- Put children's faeces in the toilet straight away.
- Wash the potty and your hands with soap.
Words to know:
- Latrine: a toilet over a pit in the ground.
- Slab: the solid floor over a pit latrine that you stand on.
- Open defecation: passing faeces in fields, bushes, rivers or other open places.
Official sources:
- WHO/UNICEF Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP): Sanitation ladder
- World Health Organization: Diarrhoeal disease fact sheet
Try it now: Check your toilet or latrine today: is it clean, covered and next to soap and water? Fix one thing. Agree with your family where children's faeces will go every time.
You can now keep a toilet or latrine clean and covered and get rid of children's faeces safely.

check.q: Where do a baby's faeces from a nappy go?
options: Into the toilet or latrine straight away
check.why: Children's faeces carry germs too and must go into the toilet.

check.q: Why keep a lid or cover on the latrine hole?
options: To keep flies from carrying germs to food
check.why: Flies that land on faeces can carry germs to food.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Diarrhoea and cholera: when to go to the clinic now
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Spot the danger signs of dehydration and cholera and get help at once.
This lesson builds toward: Given a family member with diarrhoea or watery stools, you will spot the danger signs of dehydration and cholera and take the person to the clinic at once, naming at least four danger signs and the nearest clinic or community health worker.
Diarrhoea drains water and salts from the body. This is called dehydration, and it can kill a young child quickly. Cholera can cause very large amounts of watery stool and, WHO says, can kill within hours if not treated. Do not wait to see if it gets better.
Go to the clinic, health centre or community health worker NOW if the person: is very sleepy, weak, floppy or hard to wake; cannot drink or drinks very poorly; has sunken eyes; has skin that goes back very slowly when pinched; has a lot of watery stool, like rice water; has blood in the stool; vomits again and again; or has diarrhoea that goes on for many days. A baby or young child with diarrhoea needs extra care.
Oral rehydration salts (ORS) replace the lost water and salts, and health workers also give zinc for children. Ask your clinic, community health worker or pharmacy how to use ORS; give it on the way, as they tell you, but still go. Keep breastfeeding. In a cholera outbreak, listen to your ministry of health: it may run vaccine campaigns and treatment centres. Write the name and phone number of your nearest clinic and community health worker on a card and keep money for transport if you can.
Step by step:
- Watch anyone with diarrhoea closely, especially young children.
- Check for the danger signs.
- If you see any, go to the clinic or call the community health worker now.
- Ask the health worker how to give ORS, and keep breastfeeding.
- Wash hands with soap after every contact and clean up safely.
Words to know:
- Dehydration: when the body loses too much water and salt.
- ORS (oral rehydration salts): a mix of salts and sugar that, mixed with safe water, replaces what diarrhoea takes out.
- Cholera: a disease from dirty water or food that causes very watery diarrhoea and can kill fast.
- Outbreak: many cases of an illness in one area at the same time.
Official sources:
- World Health Organization: Diarrhoeal disease fact sheet
- World Health Organization: Cholera fact sheet
Try it now: Make a danger-signs card: write four or more danger signs, the name and phone number of your nearest clinic or community health worker, and how you would get there. Put it on the wall.
You can now spot the danger signs of dehydration and cholera and get the person to the clinic at once.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Water source No source chosen, or a risky source chosen without a reason. Sources ranked with reasons; the safest chosen for drinking and a back-up named. Also notes what makes each source risky (toilets, animals, no cover) and who to tell about a broken or dirty source. Making water safer No treatment method, or a method missing steps (no boil time, no label waiting time). Boiling or a chlorine product, with settling first for cloudy water, every step and the label rule. A back-up method is planned too, and chlorine is kept out of children's reach. Storage and serving Open container, or dipping still allowed. A clean covered container, off the floor, poured or tapped, washed often. Drinking water kept separate from washing water, and everyone in the home knows the no-dipping rule. Handwashing No handwashing place or no soap; key times missing. A place with water and soap near the toilet or kitchen, and the key times written down. Places near both the toilet and the kitchen, and every family member has been shown the 20-second wash. Toilet and children's faeces Faeces left in the open or no plan for children's faeces. The toilet is kept clean and covered, and children's faeces go into it every time. A cleaning routine is shared between family members, with soap next to the toilet. Danger-signs card Fewer than four danger signs, or no clinic contact. At least four danger signs and the nearest clinic's or health worker's name and number. Also how to get there and a plan for transport money, with no medicine doses on the card. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a danger sign that means go to the clinic now?
options: A child who is very sleepy and cannot drink
check.why: Being very sleepy and unable to drink are signs of severe dehydration.

check.q: A neighbour has huge amounts of watery stool like rice water during a cholera outbreak. What do you do?
options: Give any medicine you have at home
Hide it from the health workers
Help them get to a clinic or treatment centre now
check.why: Cholera can kill within hours; fast care at a clinic saves lives.
